extracted.intended_audience: readers of philosophical treatises; students and scholars of metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Schopenhauer's account of the will as thing-in-itself, its graded objectification into phenomena (ideas, organisms, knowledge), and the teleological/teleonomic relations among parts of nature. Focus is metaphysical analysis rather than practical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental type / unité de plan (family likeness across forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a fundamental type or plan that recurs throughout nature (the 'unité de plan' or 'l’uniformité de l’élément anatomique'), which explains the family-likeness of forms across vegetable and animal kingdoms and underlies comparative anatomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as the guiding principle of modern zoological system and as a legitimate investigative aim (e.g., Schelling's school). Examples/adumbrations include Pythagorean/mathematical philosophy and the Chinese Y-king; caution noted that analogical hunts may degenerate into conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarity as a fundamental morphological/physical type
rubrics_metrics.description: Polarity—division of a force into two qualitatively opposed activities striving for reunion, often manifesting as spatial opposite directions—is a pervasive fundamental type in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by magnet/crystal/human examples and linked to Yin/Yang doctrine; flagged as a ubiquitous analogue across phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher Idea arises from conflict of lower Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple lower-grade objectifications of will conflict over matter, a higher Idea can emerge that prevails over and incorporates aspects of the lower ones, producing a more distinct, higher-grade objectification of the same will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via analogies (e.g., hardening of bones analogous to crystallisation, but not reducible to it); process involves subduing and assimilating lower forces—'no victory without conflict'—and results in a qualitatively new character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectification proceeds through graded stages (unorganised → vegetative → animal → human)
rubrics_metrics.description: The will objectifies itself in ascending grades: blind forces of unorganised nature, vegetative life (stimuli-determined), animal life (movement motivated by consciousness), and ultimately human reflective deliberation and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each grade brings new organs (e.g., brain as μηχανη) and capacities (perception, consciousness, reason). Transition to higher grades is motivated by functional need (e.g., animals must seek specific food), and phenomena such as mechanical instinct and clairvoyance illustrate overlaps between grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: No victory without conflict (higher expression requires conquest of lower forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher Idea's appearance depends on its conquest of lower Ideas; the higher manifestation endures opposition from subdued lower forces which continue to strive for expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological consequences: perpetual conflict in organisms causes fatigue, pain, need for sleep, digestion weakening faculties, and ultimately death; exemplified by magnet vs gravitation, arm dropping after effort, and the organism being 'half dead' (Jacob Böhm quote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organism's expression of Idea is attenuated by subduing lower forces
rubrics_metrics.description: An organism expresses its species-Idea only after subtracting the force expended to subdue lower physical/chemical forces; the more successful this subjection, the nearer the organism approaches its ideal/beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies seeing traces of chemical/physical operation in organisms without reducing physiology to mere chemistry; morphological/functional unity arises only after accounting for subordinated lower forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal strife: will preys upon itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Strife, conflict, and alternation of victory are ubiquitous: organisms compete for matter/space/time; animals eat plants and other animals; crystals, magnets, planetary forces all exhibit mutual opposition—this is the manifestation of will's essential variance with itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples range from ichneumon-flies, hydra budding, bulldog-ant fighting its own parts, vine strangling oak, to planetary centripetal/centrifugal tensions and crystal growth interference. Nature's existence is constituted by such struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge as μηχανη (instrument) serving the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge originates as a means (μηχανη) by which the will supports the individual and species; perceptive knowledge and reason are instruments called into being to aid the will's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In animals and most humans knowledge remains subordinated to the will; only in some individuals can knowledge free itself from serving the will, existing for its own sake (source of art) and able to prompt resignation/self-surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct versus reason: introduction of error and illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The entrance of reason and abstract conception replaces reliable instinct with deliberation, producing irresolution, uncertainty, and the possibility of error through illusive motives that mimic real ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: superstition inducing false motives (Agamemnon, miser dispensing egoistic alms expecting reward). Mechanical instincts persist among conscious beings as exceptions where blind will acts within rational behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold teleology: inner teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Inner teleology: the mutual arrangement of parts within an organism such that the sustenance of the individual and species appears as the end of that arrangement; the organism is regarded as the final end, with parts functioning as means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inner design arises because a single Idea requires a succession of parts and stages to fully express itself; unity of the Idea is re-established by necessary relations among parts (means ↔ ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold teleology: outward teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward teleology: relations between unorganised and organised nature (or among parts of organised nature) that make maintenance of the whole or a species possible, presenting themselves as means to that end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes ecological and systemic relations (plants ↔ animals ↔ planet) that enable collective sustenance; teleology here is a feature of the phenomenon (world as idea), not of thing-in-itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligible character versus empirical character (Kantian distinction applied)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligible character (timeless act of will / Idea) underlies the empirical character (manifestations in time); organisms realize their Idea through a necessary temporal succession of parts and actions, and empirical character is the time-bound expression of the timeless intelligible act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing a plant is easy (naïve, whole character in form), animals require observing actions, and humans require extensive investigation due to dissimulation afforded by reason. Kant's distinction explains freedom/necessity relations between will and phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will as the single thing-in-itself; objects are its manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite multiplicity of phenomena, only one will exists as the thing-in-itself; all objects (Ideas, species, individuals) are its manifestations, while the will itself remains unchanged amid phenomenal change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a magic-lantern's single light producing many pictures. Full manifestation of will requires the whole series of grades (man as apex plus animals/plants/unorganised as base).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of manifestations with man as apex (pyramid analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The various grades of objectification form a hierarchical pyramid in which man is the apex, complemented by animals, plants, and inorganic nature framing the complete objectification of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similes: daylight accompanied by gradations of twilight; musical analogy where melody (man/reflection) is complemented by harmony/bass (animals/nature without knowledge). This hierarchy expresses outer necessity in mutual dependence of grades.
